The results identify regimes in which semantic posterior uncertainty yields a more favorable classification--measurement trade-off and quantify the associated reconstruction cost.

title: Quantifying Long-Range Dependence in Object-Valued Time Series
text: Object-valued time series, including distributions, covariance matrices, networks, and compositions, lack the linear structure required by conventional autocovariance-based definitions of long memory. We develop an intrinsic framework for defining and estimating long memory in metric spaces of negative type. An isometric embedding yields a centered Hilbert-valued process, and the trace of its lag-covariance operator provides a signed, additive measure of temporal dependence. Crucially, this trace equals the difference between the marginal mean pairwise distance and expected lagged distance, so the framework and its estimators use only distances between the original objects. We define the memory parameter through the nonsummable decay of this trace and show that it coincides with the usual parameter in Hilbert-valued settings. Estimation uses Bartlett aggregates of distance-based lag measures. Estimating the common marginal distance from the same dependent sample induces a common-centering bias in these aggregates. We derive its finite-sample form and propose iterated block-difference corrections, log-ratio and multi-bandwidth log-slope estimators, and a localized self-consistency refinement. We establish consistency, document substantial bias reduction in simulations, and find long-memory evidence in foreign-exchange return distributions and U.S. electricity-generation compositions.

title: Concept Drift from a Causal Perspective
text: Concept drift is a common phenomenon in real-world data streams, in which changes in the data-generating distribution can degrade predictive model performance. Most existing definitions characterize drift as changes in the joint distribution formula , without distinguishing which component of the data-generating process has changed. In this work, we introduce a causal perspective on concept drift based on Structural Causal Models (SCMs). We propose a taxonomy that categorizes drift events by their causal origin, including changes in exogenous variables, endogenous mechanisms, confounders, and target-generating processes. Building on this framework, we develop an SCM-based data stream generator that simulates controlled mechanism-level drift events. Our experiments empirically characterize the distributional effects of each drift type and show that drifts with different causal origins induce distinct patterns of distribution shift and predictive behavior. Furthermore, by integrating causal discovery methods, we use our framework to construct data streams grounded in real-world dependency structures, enabling more realistic and informative evaluation scenarios. We also demonstrate that leveraging the generated data can improve downstream performance. These results highlight the importance of accounting for causal structure when studying and evaluating adaptive learning methods, and establish a foundation for causally-aware evaluation in non-stationary environments.

title: xWhyL: Causal Interactive Learning
text: Explanations are central to causal reasoning, and cognitive science has long established that the human drive to explain is itself a mechanism for learning about causality. Despite this, learning from those abductive signals is largely ignored in artificial intelligence. While explainable AI (XAI) increasingly draws on causal models to generate explanations, the converse direction about what explanations can do for causality remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we propose xWhyL, a formal framework connecting causality and XAI by learning causal models from explanations. We develop a mathematical theory that translates explanations into a learning signal complementary to observational data, and demonstrate how it enables overcoming the limits of observational causal discovery. As explanations can be derived from incorrect beliefs and clash with data, a tension we call the Causal Tug-of-War, we prove conditions under which our framework rejects misspecified explanations rather than absorbing them. Our practical instantiation, Causal Interactive Learning (CIL), shows how expert explanations can efficiently support causal discovery and distinguish correct from incorrect explanations.

title: Odd Cycle Transversal on $H$-free graphs
text: Odd Cycle Transversal is a classic formula -hard graph optimization problem asking for a minimum-weight set of vertices whose deletion makes the input graph bipartite, or equivalently, a maximum-weight induced bipartite subgraph. We show that Odd Cycle Transversal is quasi-polynomial-time solvable on formula -free graphs, for every fixed formula . In fact, we provide an formula -time algorithm for the more general Max-Weight List formula -Colorable Induced Subgraph, where the notation formula hides factors depending on formula . Paired with known results from the literature, this allows us to obtain a complete complexity dichotomy for these two problems on formula -free graphs into cases solvable in quasi-polynomial time and cases which are formula -hard, in particular resolving an open problem of Agrawal, Lima, Lokshtanov, Saurabh, and Sharma [SODA 2024]. Our algorithms are based on a new structural tool that may be of independent interest. We introduce the notion of formula -amiable family and show that, for every fixed graph formula without isolated vertices and every fixed formula , every formula -free graph admits an formula -amiable family of quasi-polynomial size that can be constructed in quasi-polynomial time. Besides yielding the aforementioned algorithms, this result gives, for every fixed connected graph formula and every fixed formula , a reduction from Max-Weight Independent Set on formula -free graphs to the same problem on formula -free graphs with formula overhead. In this setting, it improves the formula overhead obtained by specializing the general reduction of Gartland and Lokshtanov [FOCS 2020].

title: Accounting for Bias Enables Sustainable LLM Evaluation
text: LLM-as-a-judge has become the de facto standard for scalable, subjective evaluation, yet current leaderboards compensate for systematic measurement bias by running ever more comparisons, an approach that is both statistically unsound and computationally wasteful. The root cause is an incomplete measurement model, treating LLM judges as neutral, interchangeable instruments ignores documented biases like position bias, verbosity bias, judge severity, and self-enhancement, that no volume of additional data can eliminate. We propose a unified latent variable framework that jointly models pairwise and ordinal data while explicitly correcting for these confounders, recovering reliable rankings from substantially fewer comparisons. Because fitting this model costs negligible compute relative to a single round of LLM inference, bias correction is not only more statistically rigorous but also a more sustainable approach to trustworthy evaluation.

title: Scalable Variable Selection under Predictor Dependence with Adaptive Virtual Dummies
text: Reliable high-dimensional variable selection requires scalable error-controlling methods. The Terminating-Random Experiments (T-Rex) selector estimates the false discovery rate (FDR) by aggregating early-terminated forward-selection paths in which predictors compete with synthetic dummies. We address two remaining challenges: i) predictor dependence can bias dummy-predictor competition; ii) computation is wasted on recomputing terms shared across experiments. Building on memory-efficient virtual dummies, which sequentially sample projections from their exact conditional law, we estimate the conditional Gaussian law of inactive predictors and map draws onto the remaining sphere radius. A shared lazy Gram cache computes the response product and each requested Gram column once across experiments. Simulations across three covariance structures show that uniform spherical dummies can exceed the target FDR, whereas the proposed method empirically controls FDR. Caching yields more than a sixfold speedup, and the method remains feasible with 100000 predictors, where competing FDR-controlling methods become computationally impractical.

title: Computing the Helly Number, Radon Number and Rank in Cycle Convexity
text: In this paper, we investigate three fundamental convexity parameters of graphs under cycle convexity, namely the Helly number, Radon number, and rank. We first study the computational complexity of these parameters. For each of these parameters, we consider the associated threshold decision problem of determining whether the parameter of a given graph is at least a prescribed integer. We establish that all three problems are formula -hard and formula -hard when parameterized by the threshold. Moreover, we strengthen these results by showing that the formula -hardness persists even when the input is restricted to planar graphs of maximum degree at most formula . We also focus on the structural properties of connected graphs corresponding to extremal values of these parameters. In particular, we characterize the graph classes for which the three parameters attain the values formula and formula , where formula is the order of formula .

title: Reasoning with Continuous Latent Diffusion
text: We introduce the Continuous Embedding Diffusion Reasoner (CEDR), a training and inference pipeline for continuous latent diffusion models that achieves strong performance on mathematical reasoning and code generation. We learn compact answer representations from three hidden layers of the autoregressive Qwen3-4B model. A staged curriculum first trains the ELF-based diffusion backbone with teacher prompt conditioning, then initializes a compact prompt encoder through imitation and jointly adapts both networks. This replaces the large teacher contextual prompt encoder at inference with a compact learned Transformer. The multilayer answer representation also enables asynchronous inference, with different components denoised under separate clocks. We further adapt DiffusionNFT to learned self-conditioning guidance, enabling reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Controlled ablations evaluate the effects of representation design, prompt training, and denoising schedules. CEDR outperforms recent continuous-diffusion baselines at comparable backbone scales, including before reinforcement learning. With a 638M-parameter denoising backbone and DMD2-style stochastic sampling, post-NFT CEDR-L achieves pass@1, pass@8 accuracies of 68.97%, 80.82% on GSM8K and 32.40%, 53.80% on MATH500 at 64 denoising steps per sample, and 37.56%, 51.00% on HumanEval+ and 26.96%, 39.92% on MBPP+ at 128 steps per sample. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/chengxiang/CEDR and https://huggingface.co/xc91/CEDR, respectively.

title: Probability Contracts: Accuracy, Coherence, and Decisions Across LLM Interfaces
text: Equivalent probability requests can lead to different decisions even when both reports are valid. We introduce probability contracts, a benchmark that connects exact finite-world posteriors, validated event alignment, interface coherence, and failure-aware decision evaluation. Across four model-interface configurations on 1,000 worlds, Kev has lower aggregate canonical posterior error than Jev but larger complement and coarsening residuals; accuracy ordering varies by stratum. Jev's Event and Choice interfaces change the binary action on 32.8% of valid pairs at defer cost 0.10. Post-hoc analyses show that disagreement certifies only 11-52% of mean binary pair error and does not consistently outperform confidence for selection. An action-region characterization and a standard scoring-rule identity explain averaging's expected Brier guarantee relative to random interface selection, but not a decision-loss guarantee at each cost. The loss contrast takes both signs on a 99-cost grid for every configuration; small penalties where both policies beat deferral have pointwise intervals containing zero. Secondary checks specified before collection include a separate 400-root cohort, where Event/Choice effects remain configuration-dependent. A joint surface-order and answer-ID intervention shifts posttrained probabilities. Both bounded reasoning arms yield no valid probability reports, leaving their probability accuracy undefined. Probability contracts make these distinctions measurable by evaluating event semantics, posterior error, coverage, and decision cost together.

title: Low discrepancy and spectral gap for directed hypergraphs via spectral regularity lemma for tensors
text: We show that low discrepancy is equivalent to spectral gap for directed formula -uniform hypergraphs. For undirected hypergraphs this recovers a theorem of Lenz and Mubayi, with a considerably shorter proof. At the heart of our argument is a Frieze--Kannan type spectral regularity lemma for hypergraphs based on the variational notion of hypergraph eigenvalues by Friedman--Wigderson, which decomposes any tensor into a bounded number of rank-one tensors plus a quasi-random tensor with small top eigenvalue. This lemma may be of independent interest, and we prove it for complex-valued, not necessarily symmetric tensors. We also briefly discuss a Szemeredi-type variant and the regularization of Cayley-type hypergraphs over finite abelian groups.

title: Hard-Region Supervision: #1 on the Waymo Open Dataset 2D Video Panoptic Segmentation Leaderboard
text: We describe our winning entry to the Waymo Open Dataset 2D Video Panoptic Segmentation Challenge. The task asks for a semantic class at every pixel of every frame and, for countable objects, an identity that holds across 100 frames and across five overlapping cameras. We build on DVIS++, a cascade of a segmenter, a tracker, and a refiner, as our baseline. We propose hard region supervision (HRS) to improve the baseline. In particular, we use the baseline to define the hard region as where it makes mistakes, and design a loss and an auxiliary prediction head for this region. The auxiliary head is used only in training and removed at test time, so at inference the model trained with HRS has the same architecture as the baseline. In addition, we propose three test-time steps that further improve the results: a two-model ensemble, a merge of the segmenter's output into the final panoptic map, and cross-camera identity linking. On the challenge test set, our entry reaches 0.3547 wSTQ, 0.2071 wAQ, and 0.6075 mIoU, ranking first on all three metrics. It is 3.6 wSTQ points ahead of the second entry and 2.4 points ahead of our DVIS++ baseline.

title: When a Kindergartener Solves Calculus: Measuring Capability Leakage in Role-Prompted Reasoning Models
text: We investigate the problem of role-capability leakage (RCL), in which a role-prompted reasoning model generates convincing in-role text while continuing to exhibit capabilities on benchmarks that exceed those implied by the assigned role. For example, when a model is prompted to assume the role of a kindergarten student, one might expect its performance on a mathematics benchmark to reflect kindergarten-level ability rather than expert-level proficiency in solving calculus problems. We introduce RoleCapBench, a curriculum-grounded benchmark for evaluating RCL across six educational roles and four assessment levels spanning elementary school through A-level, and use it to evaluate three open-weight reasoning models. We find that although the models can generate stylistically convincing in-role responses, they consistently fail to align their underlying capabilities with their assigned roles. Naive role prompting yields strong role-voice scores of 1.218--1.389 while retaining above-role accuracy of 0.811--0.898. RCL persists across a range of prompting conditions, including prompts that explicitly instruct the model to match the role's capability level. To mitigate this problem, we propose Injection, an inference-time intervention that combines explicit, role-specific capability guidelines with a guiding prefilled response prefix. Injection improves role-capability alignment across models, reducing above-role accuracy by up to 0.562 while preserving in-role accuracy with a marginal drop of less than 0.058 across most models. All artifacts, including scripts and evaluation data, will be released upon acceptance.

title: Modelling Robust Lending Decisions under Climate Scenario Ambiguity: A Minimax-Regret Framework with NGFS Short-Term Scenarios
text: This paper develops a public-data framework for evaluating incremental bank lending when plausible climate scenarios imply different sector credit outcomes but defensible scenario probabilities are unavailable. The calibration combines 2025 Shared National Credit industry commitments, January 2026 U.S. industry leverage, interest coverage and equity volatility from Damodaran, and official 2027 sector-level probability-of-default adjustments from the NGFS CLIMACRED model. One-year Merton probabilities provide independent baseline credit-risk proxies for 16 non-financial sectors representing dollars 5.2808 trillion of commitments. Minimax regret is compared with symmetric scenario weighting and maximin under two principal decision scores: expected loss and a credit-compensation payoff using Damodaran synthetic spreads. DAPS raises the commitment-weighted one-year PD from 0.0592 to 0.0897. At a 12.5 sector cap, minimax regret reduces maximum expected-loss regret by 29.1 relative to symmetric scenario weighting; under the credit-compensation score the reduction is 69.1. Sensitivity to concentration limits, crosswalk weights, Merton inputs and the climate-PD transport shows that the value of minimax regret is conditional on scenario-specific sector rankings differing near binding portfolio constraints. The contribution is an operational decision-fragility framework for financial institutions and supervisors, not evidence about realized bank behavior or universally optimal climate lending.

title: Multi-Jurisdictional Legal Identity Assurance for Capability Gating: A Design-Science Proposal for Tiered, Reusable Identity Assurance of Natural, Juridical, and Machine Entities
text: Identity assurance is the cost a digital system pays for dishonesty and uncertainty: it exists to make acts attributable when not everyone can be trusted at their word. A common way to pay that cost is flat maximum verification, asking each participant to meet a single high level of identification at entry, before any capability is exercised. Paid on everyone, it over-collects, excludes participants who cannot meet a bar they never needed to clear, taxes every interaction with the cost of the rarest high-risk case, and binds the strength of identification to the activity it unlocks. Existing frameworks compound this by fixing a small number of per-credential levels inside a single legal space and binding each verification to the institution that performed it, leaving cross-border reuse and the tension between data erasure and evidentiary retention unaddressed. This paper develops, as a design-science proposal, a tiered and reusable model of identity assurance for natural, juridical, and machine entities across jurisdictions. Reading the problem through systems theory, where a system changes only when an entity acts, the model holds the assurance state apart from the capability gate that consumes it, so that identity demand follows the act and the weight of its consequences rather than mere presence: a participant may take part with minimal disclosure and supply more only as an act requires. It comprises a typed entity taxonomy, a two-axis coordinate of disclosed assertion scope and source of information, jurisdiction as a time-indexed attribute of the entity, and reliance recorded as bitemporal, liability-allocated, point-in-time snapshots. Requirements are derived from anti-money-laundering, electronic-identity, and data-protection law, and the proposal is evaluated against flat maximum verification, per-credential level-of-assurance designs, and institutional reusable-KYC reliance.

title: A distributional modelling approach with application to electricity price forecasting
text: The increasing volatility of electricity prices driven by renewable energy integration, market shocks, and regulatory changes has reinforced the need for forecasting methods that go beyond point predictions and accurately describe the full conditional price distribution. This paper applies the Generalised Additive Models for Location, Scale and Shape (GAMLSS) framework to forecast Spanish day-ahead electricity prices using hourly data from 2020 to 2024. Alternative specifications based on Normal, Johnson's SU (JSU), and Sinh-Arcsinh (SHASH) distributions are considered, allowing the location, scale, and shape parameters to vary with market fundamentals, including electricity demand, renewable generation, seasonal effects, and regulatory and geopolitical risk factors. Forecasts are generated using a rolling-window approach and evaluated through the mean absolute error (MAE), pinball loss, and Diebold-Mariano tests. The results show that flexible distributional specifications improve forecasting performance relative to a naive benchmark and the standard normal specification. While SHASH and JSU specifications provide the lowest point forecasting errors, the hourly analysis reveals substantial intraday variation in relative performance across specifications. JSU specification with all four parameters driven by covariates achieves the best probabilistic forecasting performance, particularly in the tails of the distribution. Diebold-Mariano tests confirm the statistical significance of these improvements. These findings highlight the importance of modelling time-varying shape distributional parameters and demonstrate the value of GAMLSS models for forecasting and risk management in increasingly volatile electricity markets.

title: Diffusion broadening of the point spread function in steady-state MRI
text: Purpose: To demonstrate how diffusion blurs the longitudinal magnetization in steady-state gradient-echo imaging, quantify resolution dependence on flip angle and repetition time, and the effects on relaxometry at microscopic resolution. Methods: Diffusion was incorporated into the Bloch-Torrey equation in formula space to determine how the point spread function (PSF) of formula -weighted spoiled gradient-echo images varies with flip angle. Theoretical predictions were validated numerically and extended to b-SSFP. Results: Diffusion acts as a low-pass filter whose width depends on the diffusion rate ( formula ), repetition time (TR), formula and flip angle ( formula ). The blurring length spans from formula at large formula to formula as formula , equaling formula at the Ernst angle. Consequently, multi-angle acquisitions have mismatched resolution (PSF widths of 39 formula m at formula versus 11 formula m at formula for TR = 50 ms). For the flip-angle pair optimizing variable-flip-angle formula mapping, the effective resolutions differ by a factor of 2.4. In simulated DESPOT1 maps the formula of a 30 formula m feature is reduced to 1.80 s formula (true value 2.00 s formula ). In b-SSFP, blurring depends on formula , formula , and formula but is independent of TR, with a minimum of formula . Conclusion: The PSF of a steady-state sequence depends on the flip angle and formula . Combining images acquired at different flip angles implicitly assumes identical spatial resolution, but that is not valid at microscopic scales, affecting the accuracy of quantitative relaxometry. The theory identifies a new limitation on the ultimate resolution of MRI set by diffusion.

title: Broken scale symmetries in undercomplete linear autoencoders
text: Neural network loss landscapes have many symmetries, which are preserved by gradient flow but broken by finite-stepsize stochastic gradient descent (SGD). A canonical example of such a symmetry is scale in homogeneous networks: one can scale up the parameters in one layer and down in the next without changing the network output. Previous work has documented cases in which SGD breaks this symmetry in favor of balancing gradient noise or minimizing fluctuations. Here, we show that the solution geometry of undercomplete linear autoencoders instead selects a preferred sign for scale drift: on the PCA solution manifold, SGD favors large decoder weights. This directed scale drift occurs on a slow timescale, and its dynamics admit an analytically-tractable effective description. However, it cannot continue indefinitely: increasing scale eventually drives the dynamics towards a finite-stepsize stability boundary. The resulting solutions are sharper than a balanced baseline in the sense of the maximum eigenvalue of the loss Hessian, but different sharpness measures can move in opposing directions. Thus, undercomplete autoencoders give a concrete illustration of how loss geometry can convert residual gradient noise into directed motion along a manifold of functionally-equivalent solutions.

title: Latent-driven Imputation and Forecasting for partially observed Time Series (LIFTS)
text: Partially observed multivariate time series pose two coupled challenges: recovering missing measurements and forecasting future trajectories when observation patterns are informative. Existing methods often assume ignorable missingness or use the mask only as an auxiliary input. We propose LIFTS (Latent-driven Imputation and Forecasting for partly observed Time Series), a probabilistic framework in which a latent process jointly governs the complete measurement trajectory and observation mask, allowing observation patterns to inform latent-state inference for both forecasting and imputation. LIFTS combines flexible neural-network parameterizations with a forward-backward architecture: the forward pass performs filtering and autoregressive forecasting, while the backward pass performs smoothing and conditional multiple imputation. The model and inference components are trained jointly using a masked energy score and self-masking. We establish forward-backward distributional representations for the general framework and, for an explicit structural subclass, provide full-law identification and consistency guarantees. Simulations and an application to PhysioNet 2019 show that LIFTS provides accurate point predictions, improved distributional accuracy, and well-calibrated predictive intervals; it outperforms competing methods particularly when training data are limited and has substantially faster inference than the diffusion-based baseline.

title: Wiener Space Cubature for Nonlinear Gaussian Filtering
text: Continuous-discrete filtering is a classical problem in signal processing and control theory, whereby the state driving a stochastic differential equation (SDE) must be inferred from noisy, partial discrete-time observations. Corresponding filtering algorithms are often formed as discrete-time methods and applied to a discretization of the SDE, an approach limited by the incurred discretization error, or model a type of Gaussian moment ordinary differential equation (ODE) flow, which is approximate for nonlinear dynamics. We introduce a new method, the Wiener-space cubature Kalman filter (WSC-KF), for Gaussian filtering in this continuous-discrete setting. The WSC-KF combines spatial sigma-point representations with Wiener space cubature integration, effectively approximating iterated integral terms of the driving Brownian motion to higher-order than standard discretization (e.g., Ito-Taylor expansions), or approximate moment-ODE flows (e.g., as in the unscented Kalman filter). Theoretically, we characterize the path-law approximation degree of WSC-KF through a tunable model order parameter. We prove that, depending on the model order chosen, WSC-KF provides weak order bounds comparable to or dominating that of a cubature Kalman filter using a first-order Ito predict step. Numerically, we confirm that rate on a globally Lipschitz Levy-area diffusion. Degree-5 Wiener cubature matches mixed iterated integrals that existing continuous-discrete Kalman predictors omit, while remaining efficiently computable; this is the mechanism enabling higher-order weak path-law approximation.

title: Conformal Risk Control for Multiuser Beamforming
text: We consider multiuser downlink beamforming with prescribed signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) requirements under imperfect channel state information and a tight transmit power budget. Robust worst-case designs often require tractable channel-error models and may not yield feasible beamformers that meet the power budget. To alleviate these issues, we propose conformal risk control for beamforming (CRCBeam), which combines the classical fixed-point minimum-power beamforming with conformal risk control to calibrate an SINR margin from calibration sample pairs of estimated and true channels. Under exchangeability, CRCBeam provides finite-sample control over served-outage risk, which is the probability of transmitting when at least one user fails to meet its SINR target. CRCBeam requires no parametric channel-error model and transmits only when the power budget is met. Numerical experiments using a pilot contamination channel error model corroborate that CRCBeam achieves the served-outage risk while meeting the power budget. In contrast, worst-case robust baselines, Gaussian-ball and conformal-ball beamforming, either do not meet the target risk or exceed the power budget.

title: Payment Design under Belief Disagreement: Rent Placement, Bid Resolution, and Auction Choice
text: When auction bidders misperceive their rivals, a seller can change not only the amount of information rent but also the states in which it is delivered. We ask when this payment-design opportunity survives a finite bidding interface, nonnegative-payment restrictions, and comparison with conventional auctions under the same beliefs. We formulate payment design as a linear program in nonnegative bidder rents. A single state can safely carry a report's rent when it is both cheapest for its intended type and least attractive to potential mimics. We characterize this alignment, bound the cost of a restricted payment architecture when alignment is imperfect, and use shadow prices when the rankings conflict. Own-type projection yields a unique optimal expected-payment rule for a fixed allocation. Contiguous bid bands implement truthful reporting at every value, but create pooling losses and within-band surplus. Under a separate smooth-belief model, feasible truthful rules and revenue upper bounds support comparisons with a first-price equilibrium under the same beliefs. A calibration using 1,000 eBay proof-set auction records illustrates a partition-dependent reversal: first price dominates all exactly truthful, no-subsidy rules on ten equal-probability bands in one scenario, while a richer contingent rule on ten equal-dollar bands outperforms it. An operator should choose interface resolution, payment dependence, and integrity tolerances jointly. Validate the probabilities that support incentives, compare formats under the same beliefs, and distinguish redesign from deployment. Any receipt advantage must cover implementation costs before it can imply a profit advantage.

title: Learned Monotone Recurrent Features in Governed Credit Scoring: The Price of the Frame and the Necessity of Macro Conditioning
text: Regulated credit scoring requires scores monotone non-decreasing in every exposure input. Deployed pipelines -- hand-crafted monotone aggregates feeding sign-constrained gradient boosting -- already meet this by composition; the open question is what learned temporal aggregation is worth inside one. We answer on five production-scale credit datasets at matched admissibility (one priced baseline convention excepted), with a monotone recurrent architecture whose per-input guarantee we extend, with proofs, to vector-valued inputs and to exogenously macro-conditioned decay gates, severities, thresholds, and peak memory. Two findings result. First, a strictness ladder: the value of learned monotone features rises with governance-frame strictness -- zero on unconstrained engineered panels, maximal in summaries-only frames -- replicated across two datasets and an official temporal-stability metric, though unconditioned features degrade on externally adjudicated later weeks. Second, a conditioning-delivery asymmetry under regime shift. On a train-on-boom, test-on-crisis mortgage design, two public macroeconomic series hurt as input columns, yet conditioning the recurrence on them delivers the paper's only learned-block crisis-cohort uplifts. The confirmed effect: +0.006 to +0.013 AUC on an internally pre-registered Freddie Mac replication, at all five held-out seeds. The discovery estimate: +0.015 to +0.021 on Fannie Mae (three of five seeds post hoc), worth 10-27 basis points of defaulted balance at an 80% approval cutoff, and grows with early-prepaid loans excluded. A state-level test identifies the mechanism: between-cohort calibration transfer. A pandemic-band episode bounds scope: under forbearance-distorted labels the gain generalizes at a quarter to a third of crisis size on Fannie Mae, on Freddie Mac only against the capacity control.

title: Dolbeault Cohomology Growth under Curvature Rank Bounds
text: Let formula be a smooth Hermitian holomorphic line bundle on a compact complex manifold formula of dimension formula , and let formula be its maximal curvature rank. For every fixed holomorphic vector bundle formula , we prove formula for every formula and every Dolbeault degree, with the sharp bounds formula at the endpoints. The curvature may have variable rank and arbitrary signature, and no global foliation or Kahler assumption is imposed. The all-degree estimate follows from local rescaling and holomorphic restriction estimates that remain uniform across rank changes. An independent maximum-principle argument locates the maximal rank of a section map at a semipositive curvature point; it yields formula on each connected component formula and gives the endpoint bounds.

title: PageWeaver: KV-Guided Query Unions for Sparse Attention
text: Dynamic sparse attention limits the KV pages selected by each query, but a small support does not necessarily yield efficient GPU work. Query unions share page loads and populate Tensor Core tiles; their cost depends on which queries are grouped together. We present PageWeaver, an execution design that uses selected-page affinity to assemble query groups while preserving each query's original support and complete output ownership. A bounded GPU search produces query IDs, and an ID-aware two-CTA kernel consumes them without materializing reordered Q tensors or cross-page partial outputs. A direct KV-page union implementation provides a complementary design study of nonlocal reuse and reduction cost. With FP8 KV throughout, the H200 Union8 implementation achieves a 1.70x geometric-mean complete-call speedup over the measured FlashInfer path on six captures. Online regrouping further lowers latency by 3.26-7.66% on five selected 64K-context captures. Whole-model prefill throughput is 7.88-14.36% above the tested native path; the incremental regrouping benefit is smaller, with observed median gains of 0.47-0.73% at 32K/64K and regressions at 8K. A B300 comparison identifies cases where preparation cost and a stronger native kernel remove the advantage. These results separate execution-group reuse from the complete cost of exploiting it online.

title: An efficient stochastic generalized method of moments estimator for nonlinear moment models
text: We study the asymptotic properties of the nonlinear stochastic GMM algorithm proposed by Chen, Lee, Liao, Seo, Shin and Song for recursively estimating parameters defined by possibly nonlinear and overidentified moment restrictions formula . Each observation updates estimates of the moment Jacobian, inverse covariance matrix and Gauss--Newton preconditioner at a cost independent of sample size. For linear and nonlinear instrumental-variable moments, we derive an exact rank-two Sherman--Morrison--Woodbury update. The algorithm combines preconditioned stochastic approximation with iterate averaging. Under a preconditioned monotonicity condition, satisfied globally in linear models and locally around a consistent pilot estimate in general, we establish almost sure convergence and rates, as well as a functional central limit theorem with the efficient GMM variance. These results require four moments of the moment function and its Jacobian when the step exponent exceeds formula . The inverse Gauss--Newton matrix consistently estimates this variance, and a projected linearised statistic enables online testing of overidentifying restrictions. We extend the results to formula -dependent data with long-run variance weights under stronger moment assumptions. Simulations show that the averaged estimator approaches offline two-step GMM in accuracy and coverage at formula observations, while requiring a fraction of its computing time and fixed memory at up to formula observations. The online test achieves correct size and comparable power. In an application estimating the effect of a third child on weeks worked using formula women from the 1980 US Census, single-pass estimates agree with offline GMM within a fraction of a standard error on average across data orderings, and both methods yield the same overidentification-test conclusion in most orderings.

title: Tail Instability and Scale Control in Conditional Normalizing Flows for Treasury Yield-Curve Scenarios
text: A conditional normalizing flow can produce extreme scenarios even when its point forecasts appear reasonable. We compare two fitted models for daily Treasury yield changes at eleven maturities reconstructed from Federal Reserve curve parameters. Both use an LSTM, an auxiliary location head, and an affine residual flow. On a previously unused 60-date window, the frozen Student-t model generated an absolute standardized coordinate of 34.3 million. A Gaussian-base model with tighter coupling scale control reached 14.72. Each generated 600,000 vectors. The original model's scenario-mean MSE was 33,908.95, while its location-head MSE was 0.3376. The stabilized model's two estimates remained close. Across five development windows, the stabilized maximum was 17.33 among three million vectors. Stability did not imply better prediction: historical simulation had better distributional scores and coverage closer to nominal on the new window. The original flow also had a better log score despite its extreme samples. Frozen-model evaluation is reproducible, but the comparison does not isolate architectural effects or establish a general forecasting advantage.

title: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
text: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.

title: DISARM-ing the Hidden Puppetmaster: An Interface for Exposing Manipulative Tactics in Large Language Models
text: Large language models (LLMs) can covertly steer users' beliefs through emotionally manipulative tactics, yet little is known about how interfaces can protect users as such influence unfolds. We investigate whether in-situ disclosures can inoculate users against manipulation during AI conversations. Following a formative study, we developed DISARM, an interface that identifies, explains, and tracks manipulative tactics and hidden incentives. We evaluated our interface in a between-subjects experiment where 488 participants sought advice from an LLM pursuing a harmful hidden objective, with or without disclosures from DISARM. Participants receiving disclosures exhibited 78% less belief shift toward the agent's objective and perceived its advice as more biased and less actionable and the agent as less ethical, reliable, and well-intentioned. An inductive analysis of 1,927 user turns identified 16 response and pushback strategies. We contribute evidence that real-time disclosures can reduce manipulative influence, design recommendations for resistance, and a dataset of categorized responses.

title: MetaExp: Learning to Self-Improve through Experience via Verifiable Cross-Task Environment Scaling
text: Language-model agents can accumulate interaction feedback, but reliably turning that feedback into reusable experience remains challenging. Existing methods either optimize external experience scaffolds or train experience-related behavior on specific task distributions, leaving open whether experience learning itself can become a transferable model capability. Training such a capability calls for supervision beyond isolated tasks, which mainly support in-episode problem solving rather than revealing what knowledge remains useful across episodes. In this work, we introduce MetaExp, a scalable framework that trains this capability through verifiable task families with controlled cross-task structure. Each family preserves a reusable factor while varying task-specific realizations, enabling transfer without direct solution reuse. We propose two complementary designs: Shared-Tool families keep black-box tools fixed across tasks to elicit operational experience, while Shared-Workflow families preserve latent procedures across changing realizations to elicit procedural experience. We scale environments under both designs, collect and filter sequential interaction trajectories, and fine-tune Qwen3.5-122B-A10B on 4,956 trajectories from 1,000 task families. With parameters frozen during downstream evolution, MetaExp improves by +8.5 points on SpreadsheetBench, peaks at +2.3 on APEX-Agents, and improves by +14.8 on AutomationBench. The gains persist under domain-excluded training, supporting experience learning as a transferable capability for continued non-parametric improvement after deployment.

title: Short-Boundary Signaling for Asynchronous Grant-Free Control-to-Control Communications
text: In asynchronous grant-free access, receivers must detect variable-length transmissions and identify their start and end. Existing decoder-aided receivers use start and tail sequences which are as long as one codeword, causing substantial overhead for short commands. This paper treats the boundary (i.e., start and tail sequences) length as an independent design parameter and proposes a convolutional neural network that detects both boundaries from the received waveform and the decoder soft output. Its waveform input size decreases with the boundary length, while the decoder input keeps the codeword length, so the boundary can be shortened without altering the decoder. Analysis and simulations quantify the resulting tradeoff among payload efficiency, collision exposure, and boundary detection. The results show that the proposed receiver can exploit very short boundaries: in the considered setting, the shortest tested boundary, formula , yields the highest effective payload efficiency at all tested loads, whereas a correlation-based benchmark with the same sequences performs best with formula at moderate and high loads.

title: Designing Experiments for External Decision Makers
text: Standard Bayesian experimental design (BED) methods assume the experimenter alone will act on the data, choosing the best action given their own beliefs and goals. In practice, data are often acted on by external parties whose procedures the experimenter cannot change and may not know, particularly when the data are released publicly. To extend BED to such settings, we introduce usage-aware experimental design, a framework in which an adaptive design policy is trained to minimise the usage risk: the experimenter's expected loss when one or more external rules act on the collected data. These rules may be non-Bayesian or black-box, and when several may apply, we either average over them or take the worst case. We show that, unlike in standard BED, more informative data can be harmful under such rules, so the usage risk cannot in general be expressed as an expected uncertainty reduction; our framework thus strictly generalises standard BED. We then use it to tackle a range of problems that are difficult to address with existing approaches.

title: Retrospective Evaluation of Bluetooth RSSI Fingerprinting for Bin Localization on an Industrial Shop Floor
text: This paper evaluates an archival Bluetooth Low Energy received signal strength indicator (RSSI) dataset collected for bin localization on an industrial shop floor. The installation used 24 fixed relays positioned on walls and Bluetooth beacons attached to bins, with each relay applying a Kalman filter to its own readings in firmware before publishing them. The primary survey produced 19,034 usable two-minute fingerprint samples across 90 known positions, with 23 relay measurements available as model features. We compare calibrated path-loss multilateration with two radio-map estimators: distance-weighted formula -nearest neighbours and Random Forest regression. A random 70/30 row split measures recognition at surveyed positions, while a coordinate-grouped split reserves 27 entire positions for testing and measures interpolation to unseen positions. Random Forest achieved a median error of 0.66~m for surveyed positions, with 77.9% of estimates within 3~m and 96.3% within 10~m. For unseen positions, median error increased to 9.42~m and 55.5% of estimates were within 10~m. Path-loss multilateration produced a 19.41~m median error on unseen positions, close to the 19.62~m mean-position baseline. The results support RSSI fingerprinting for a fixed inventory of surveyed bin positions, but not precise continuous localization between survey points. Git history dates the original implementation to September 7, 2019. The evaluation code in this paper was written in October 2026 and is reported separately from the seven-year-old prototype.

title: Critical cusp cancellation and analytic response for a Bernoulli random interval map
text: We show that the critical cusp exponent formula admits formula invariant densities in an explicit family of expanding full-branch interval maps. The usual estimates exclude this exponent because two zero-order coefficients in the second derivative of the transfer operator are individually non-integrable. Their signed combination, however, contains the factor formula for a pure power cusp. We exploit its cancellation at formula to prove a formula Lasota--Yorke inequality and a spectral gap for the explicit family. We also identify a separate obstruction caused by an interior cusp value. As an application, a small Bernoulli probability perturbation between two fixed maps has a stationary density that depends real-analytically on the perturbation parameter in formula , with explicit formulas for all response derivatives.

title: The wealth-to-salary ratio: a simple indicator of inequality
text: In previous studies, using agent-based simulations of a model of a capitalist economy proposed by Ian Wright, we showed that inequality in both wealth and income distributions is largely governed by a single key parameter: the ratio between average wealth per capita and the mean salary, denoted by formula . This parameter captures the relative importance of accumulated assets compared with labor income. In the model, larger values of formula are systematically associated with higher levels of inequality, as measured by the Gini coefficient. In the present work, we investigate whether this relationship is also observed in real-world economies. Using empirical data from the World Inequality Database (WID) and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), we construct empirical estimates of formula and compare them with standard measures of income and wealth inequality. We find a positive relation between formula and inequality across several empirical settings, with the strongest relationships observed for mature and advanced economies. These results provide empirical support for the role of the wealth-to-salary ratio as a simple macroscopic indicator associated with economic inequality, while also highlighting the limitations imposed by differences in data definitions and measurement across countries and periods.

title: Rating Multiple Agents with Career Concerns
text: A principal designs ratings for multiple career-concerned agents with correlated talents, mapping outputs into arbitrary finite-variance statistics. Peer output both benchmarks effort and signals talent, making full disclosure suboptimal under confidential ratings. Relaxing Bayes plausibility to linear orthogonality yields a closed-form rating and computable effort bounds for general priors; under normality, the relaxation is exact. Optimal confidential ratings combine the full-disclosure wage with the Fisher score for effort: they are relative-performance when individual output is informative about talent and team-based when it is noisy. Public ratings must satisfy joint Bayes plausibility, weakening incentives; hence, the principal prefers confidential ratings, whereas agents prefer public ratings. A spectral decomposition characterizes public ratings under normality: small cost heterogeneity implies full disclosure regardless of the noise structure, whereas large cost heterogeneity or strong effort spillovers can induce partial disclosure to reallocate incentives. The results bear on performance ratings and pay transparency.

title: The four-dimensional Sklyanin algebras revisited
text: We give a theta-function and projective-geometric account of the four-dimensional Sklyanin algebras. We define a family of quadratic algebras by declaring that their relations are precisely the two-tensors vanishing on the graph of a translation automorphism on a quartic complex elliptic curve and the vertex pairs where the vertices are the singular points of the four singular quadrics that contain it. We then use Jacobi's addition formulas for theta functions to produce a set of six explicit relations that coincide with Sklyanin's RLL-relations associated to Baxter's elliptic solutions to the 2 x 2 Yang-Baxter equation. We use the geometric definition to show that these algebras coincide with Feigin and Odesskii's four-dimensional elliptic algebras. Our approach agrees with that of Rains-Ruijsenaars theta function perspective on the four-dimensional Sklyanin agebras. For example, the rank-two secant-line relations of Levasseur-Smith coincide with their two-variable theta function relations. We give explicit theta-function formulas for the degree-two central elements, previously obtained by Levassuer-Smith, that annihilate various families of line modules.

title: Learnable Pilot Design for OFDM-based Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding
text: Recent advances in deep joint source-channel coding (DeepJSCC) have shown strong robustness to channel variations in wireless image transmission. However, its integration with orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) typically relies on fixed pilot patterns that are not optimized for receiver- side channel processing. This work introduces Pilot-Efficient DeepJSCC-OFDM (PE-JSCC), which learns pilot placement under a strictly fixed number of pilot symbols via a Gumbel- Top-k-based selector. The learned pilot placement improves end- to-end performance over the conventional Block-JSCC, Comb- JSCC, and Scatter-JSCC baselines. To support high mobility, the receiver incorporates a lightweight axial-attention-based inter- carrier interference (ICI) canceler and a CNN-based channel estimator. Simulation results show that PE-JSCC consistently outperforms fixed pilot patterns across diverse SNRs and remains robust over a wide mobility range.

title: On the Vulnerabilities and Data-Free Removal of Watermarks in Batch Normalization Layers
text: Batch Normalization (BN) layers have become a common choice for embedding white-box watermarks in Federated Learning (FL), providing a simple and effective mechanism for model ownership verification and participant identification. However, previous works have focused on robustness against generic model modifications, leaving the security implications of this design largely unexplored. In this paper, we identify fundamental vulnerabilities of BN-based watermarking schemes and propose a practical data-free attack that exploits them. Experimental results on two representative FL watermarking schemes show that the proposed attack consistently removes the watermark with minimal impact on model performance, even without access to representative training data. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of evaluating DNN watermarking schemes under threat models consistent with Kerckhoffs's principle, rather than relying on security through obscurity.

title: Fields on accelerating and super accelerating black holes: stability, quasinormal modes, greybody factors and strong cosmic censorship
text: We investigate the propagation of massless scalar, Dirac, and Maxwell fields on accelerating and super accelerating black hole spacetimes described by the C-metric. The latter regime has only recently been identified and remains largely unexplored. We study the linear and mode stability of these backgrounds and derive analytical expressions for the quasinormal mode spectra and greybody factors in various spacetime limits. We classify the quasinormal mode families, paying particular attention to new families arising in the super accelerating regime. We also investigate strong cosmic censorship through Christodoulou's formula criterion, finding regions of parameter space where it may be violated, including in the super accelerating regime. These violations are possible for massless scalar and Maxwell fields, whereas Dirac fields preserve the conjecture.

title: Generalized CycleGRPO for Fine-Grained Multimodal Understanding and Grounding
text: Fine-grained multimodal intelligence requires models to both understand a designated region and localize it from language. Existing methods learn these directions with separate objectives and task-specific annotations. We present Generalized CycleGRPO, the first unified reinforcement learning framework coupling region understanding and localization across spatial, temporal, and spatio-temporal domains. Given a region, a multimodal large language model generates candidate descriptions and then localizes each description to reconstruct the input region. Reconstruction overlap provides a verifiable reward for captioning, while individual localization rewards improve the inverse mapping. A common region-space formulation extends this cycle from image masks and boxes to video intervals and timestamped spatial evidence, without reference captions or an external language-model judge during reinforcement learning. In videos, the cycle encourages descriptions that distinguish a target event from similar recurrences. We introduce DOVE (Distinctive Occurrence-level Video-caption Evaluation), a human-verified contrastive benchmark for this temporal distinctiveness. CycleGRPO improves SAMTok's overall gIoU from 57.5% to 68.2% on GroundingSuite and average gIoU from 71.2% to 78.7% on GRES. For temporal tasks, it achieves 51.9% tIoU on Charades and 33.3% Temporal Evidence Coverage on DOVE, compared with 45.6% and 14.8% for the Qwen3-VL initialization. These results establish region-text cycle consistency as a general self-evaluation principle for multimodal understanding and localization. Models, code, and DOVE are available at https://devinxzhang.github.io/Generalized-CycleGRPO-Page/.

title: Integrated Longitudinal and Lateral Control for High-Speed Platooning of Articulated Vehicles
text: This paper presents an integrated control framework for high-speed platooning of articulated vehicles, combining advanced longitudinal and lateral control strategies to address the challenges of safe and efficient autonomous driving. A novel proof of string stability for the proposed longitudinal control algorithm, based on a PID framework, ensures robust inter-vehicle distance regulation even under dynamic operating conditions. Additionally, an arc-length-based longitudinal error formulation enhances the applicability of the control system for curved roads, making it realistic for diverse driving scenarios. For lateral control, significant improvements to the clothoid-based path tracking algorithm are introduced to mitigate oscillations and enhance stability at high speeds. These enhancements include a tangential criterion for oscillation reduction, trajectory segment classification for adaptive lookahead distance tuning, a dual-adaptive mechanism for regulating the rate of lookahead distance adjustments based on both cross-track error (CTE) and anticipated road curvature, and extensions for articulated vehicle dynamics. The proposed integrated control framework is validated through simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining stability, minimizing tracking errors, and ensuring robust performance in high-speed and challenging platooning scenarios.

title: Estimating Group Average Treatment Effects in High-Risk Populations with Unobserved Target Membership
text: Estimating treatment effects within a prespecified high-risk population is challenging. When risk status is unobserved or the target population is small, analyses restricted to high-risk individuals can be unstable or inefficient. We propose a risk-score-weighted soft-targeting (RSW) estimator for group average treatment effects in high-risk populations. It accommodates two settings: when high-risk status is observed, the membership probability can be estimated within the analysis sample; when unobserved, it can be obtained from a reference model using covariates in the analysis sample. RSW uses these probabilities to represent the target population, learns a doubly robust treatment effect in the full sample, and aggregates a low-dimensional treatment-effect surface over the risk-weighted target distribution. We establish pointwise asymptotic normality and an influence-function-based variance estimator. In simulations with continuous and binary outcomes, RSW had similar bias and lower variance than two hard-targeting alternatives. Sensitivity analyses showed that the gain persisted when treatment-effect sufficiency was violated, although RSW bias increased under strong violations. We applied the method to the All of Us study to estimate effects of non-GLP antidiabetic and antihypertensive medication use on mild cognitive impairment (MCI)-free time restricted at 48 months within comorbidity-defined high-risk subgroups. We estimated the risk score in a nonoverlapping internal reference sample and applied it to the outcome-analysis sample. This illustrates how soft targeting can improve precision while retaining an interpretable high-risk target population.

title: DBCM: Dual-Branch Calibration Module for Test-Time Adaptation in Time Series Forecasting
text: Non-stationarity induces test-time distribution shifts in time series forecasting (TSF), resulting in forecast residuals between predictions and the corresponding ground truth. Recent works on test-time adaptation for TSF address this by introducing lightweight calibration modules around frozen forecasters, updated using observations that become incrementally available at test time. Existing approaches typically employ channel-wise adapters, implicitly assuming that forecast residuals are inherently channel-specific. However, we observe that forecast residuals often exhibit substantial shared structure across channels, suggesting that fully independent channel-wise parameterization may be redundant. Motivated by this observation, we propose the Dual-Branch Calibration Module (DBCM), which shares adaptation capacity across channels through a shared adapter while retaining limited channel-specific flexibility through a low-rank channel-wise adapter, further enhanced by channel mixing and nonlinear gated modulation. Extensive experiments show that DBCM consistently outperforms prior methods across diverse datasets, horizons, and backbones.

title: Pesin's entropy formula on attractors with continuous invariant splittings
text: Under quantitative asymptotic hyperbolicity assumptions, we prove the existence of hyperbolic ergodic invariant probability measures satisfying Pesin's entropy formula for formula diffeomorphisms whose attractors admit extendable continuous invariant splittings. No dominated splitting is required on the attractor. For formula diffeomorphisms, the resulting measures are SRB measures. Our results apply to mostly expanding partially hyperbolic systems and to systems with strictly separated Lyapunov exponents under suitable statistical assumptions. We also construct examples with hyperbolic SRB measures of full support on attractors admitting no nontrivial dominated splitting, demonstrating the applicability of our criteria beyond results that require domination.

title: Compiling and forecasting implied volatility surfaces via survey sampling, tempered inverse-probability sequence learning, and causal activity clocks
text: Compiling implied volatility (IV) surfaces and forecasting derivative risk from high-frequency equity and options feeds requires addressing contract heterogeneity, schema shifts, volatility clustering, and non-stationary trading activity. Using a split-adjusted NVIDIA (NVDA) equity and options panel (2018-2025), this study integrates finite-population survey sampling, tempered inverse-probability sequence learning, and causal activity clocks. Four findings emerge. First, cross-sectional surface accuracy depends on matching the sampling design to the target functional: plug-in stratified allocations using lagged cell dispersion improve equal-weighted surface reconstruction with full grid coverage, whereas liquidity-weighted probability proportional to size (PPS) sampling excels on liquidity-weighted targets by construction yet inflates error when misapplied. Second, in longitudinal LSTM sequence training, PPS and Neyman designs retain more tail-volatility windows than simple random sampling (SRS); all three designs are equivalent to full-census training within chosen margins while cutting training time, though incremental forecasting gains of informative selection over SRS are not established. Third, out-of-sample evaluation shows a predictability contrast: short-horizon prices are not forecastable beyond a random walk with drift among tested models, whereas forward IV shows descriptive mean-reversion skill concentrated in a few post-shock reversal sessions (insignificant under session-clustered tests), with sequence models not beating a linear HAR-IV benchmark and feature pruning driving stability. Fourth, across a 6.3x start-to-end (nearly twentyfold trough-to-peak) price expansion, rolling volume and dollar clocks stabilize bar rates and compress intraday return kurtosis beyond diurnal scaling.

title: InteractiveWorld: A Verifiable Human-Centric Environment for Building Better Interactive MLLM Assistants
text: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

title: Refined analysis on finite-time singularities of almost-holomorphic harmonic map flow
text: Building on the work of Song--Waldron~ SongWaldron2024, we establish stronger regularity and refined blow-up analysis results for almost-holomorphic harmonic map flow from a closed surface into a compact Kahler manifold with nonnegative holomorphic bisectional curvature. At each finite-time singularity, we improve the outer energy scale to formula . We also prove that both the stress-energy tensor and the tension field converge strongly in formula to those of the body map, by ruling out concentration of their formula energy near the singular points. Consequently, the body map belongs to formula . Finally, an explicit gap theorem for the antiholomorphic energy of nonholomorphic harmonic spheres yields an explicit admissible threshold for the initial antiholomorphic energy under which these conclusions hold.

title: Smart charging without rebound peaks: Wholesale price feedback limits distribution grid peaks from price-responsive electric vehicles
text: Studies on price-optimized EV charging consistently find that the common price signal synchronizes charging of the entire fleet of cars in the cheapest hours and creates new "rebound" load peaks in low-voltage grids. Almost all of these studies treat wholesale prices as exogenous, i.e., unaffected by the shifting EV load. This paper argues that this assumption overstates the problem: charging in low-price hours raises the wholesale price in those hours, which spreads charging across hours in equilibrium. I simulate price-optimized charging under real-time prices calibrated to German 2025 data. Even when adjusting for the increase in electricity demand, the coincident import peak of the local grid rises by 260%. After adding a model of equilibrium wholesale prices that takes the price-quantity feedback into account, the increase is reduced to a mere 5%. Allowing for vehicle-to-grid, the export peak rises by 115% and falls by 6%, respectively. The result holds across vehicle and charging parameters, charging constraints, renewable scenarios, network charges, price functions, peak measures, and simulation assumptions. Rebound peaks remain possible where vehicle adoption runs ahead of the national average or where charging power is high, but they are much smaller than the literature consensus suggests.

title: Well located Banach spaces - A combined approach to L_1- preduals and Hilbert space
text: In the description of L_1- preduals on the one hand and of Hilbert spaces, on the other, one encounters the surprising appearance of similar classes of operators in terms of their extendibility properties in the setting of these two classes of spaces. It also turns out that the extension properties are closely tied to how the two classes of spaces are positioned inside the ambient spaces. It is well known that in the case of all subspaces being positioned inside a larger space Z as a complemented subspace leads to Z being (isomorphically) a Hilbert space whereas in the case of a Banach space X which is complemented inside all its superspaces, it turns out that X is an injective Banach space. In this paper, we shall be concerned mostly with such properties as demanding that X sit inside the ambient space as a locally complemented subspace (and sometimes as a Lipchitz retract). It turns out that the class of Banach spaces X determined by the indicated properties are precisely the class of L_1- preduals in the former case and of Hilbert spaces, in the latter. As an important consequence of this approach, we are led to several new characterisations of Hilbert spaces in terms of the extendibility of bounded linear maps coming from well-known operator (nonlinear operator) ideals.

title: Spectral zeta functions in positive characteristic
text: Spectral zeta functions and zeta-regularized determinants encode the spectrum of an operator in analytic functions. Over the completion formula of an algebraic closure of formula , two features of characteristic formula break this classical picture. Complex powers have exponents that vary only continuously in formula , not analytically. Scalar traces record eigenvalue multiplicities only modulo formula . We develop a resolvent-based theory that treats these two obstructions separately. For the first, inverse Stieltjes duality turns suitable scalar resolvents into locally analytic spectral distributions on formula . A single exponent of the Mellin transform already determines the distribution and the entire Mellin family. We characterize exactly which power series arise in this way, by a growth condition on Carlitz moments. The criterion depends on the support: bounded Taylor coefficients are not sufficient. For stationary digit measures, the transform is the unique fixed point of an explicit contraction. The first formula nonconstant moments recover the measure. For the second, we replace traces by the Frobenius defect formula , where formula raises coefficients to their formula th powers. On power series with small coefficients, this map is a group automorphism that preserves Gauss distances, and a convergent infinite product inverts it. Polynomial defects produce entire functions. They characterize exactly the diagonal spectra that are finite unions of forward Frobenius orbits, counted with multiplicity. For the shifted Carlitz operator, the resulting Fredholm determinant is a normalized reciprocal of the Anderson--Thakur function, and its Newton polygon is determined exactly.

title: Beyond "[at]": A Large-Scale Measurement of Email Address Presentation on Computer Science Scholars' Homepages
text: Publishing an email address makes a scholar reachable, but also exposes it to automated collection. Yet how email addresses are presented on the Web has not been measured systematically across their content, form, and location. We measure it across 32,413 homepage records of computer-science scholars listed in CSRankings with MailScope, which preserves raw and rendered HTML, extracts addresses with a three-stage cascade (rules, then large language models, then a crawling agent), and labels each address. Among 19,517 reachable homepages, we find an address for 17,712 scholars (90.8%). Our measurement yields four main findings. (i) Presentation is diverse: only 53.8% publish plain content, the others spread over 23 subtypes of symbol substitution, code, and semantic description, and 5.5% of scholars' addresses appear only after rendering. (ii) Presentation follows hosts rather than individuals: scholars on one host share a content class in 67.9% of pairs, compared with 38.8% across hosts of one institution, whereas research output and institution rank are barely related to presentation. (iii) Content and form are coupled through code-based links, and 6.2% of scholars with non-plain selected presentations have plain-text copies of the same address elsewhere. (iv) Plain addresses are more common behind passed bot challenges, and 36.1% of redirecting homepages no longer lead to scholars. Human assessment yields 94.4% weighted exact-set agreement on 143 judgeable pages, complemented by three 500-page review rounds with human verification. Presentation is diverse but clusters by shared host, and by our label-based estimate plain-string matching misses nearly half of the addresses.

title: DRC-TTS: A Dual-Resolution Codec-Based Architecture for Lexicon-Free Malay Speech Synthesis
text: Modern discrete neural audio codecs facilitate speech synthesis by replacing continuous acoustic representations with low-frame-rate discrete token sequences. For Malay speech synthesis, character-level input reduces reliance on pronunciation lexicons. However, combining character-level inputs with low-frame-rate discrete codecs introduces a temporal alignment challenge. When predicted character durations are quantized into frame counts at 12.5 Hz, durations shorter than one codec frame may be assigned zero frames. Consequently, the corresponding character representations may be lost during length regulation, potentially leading to pronunciation omissions. This study proposes DRC-TTS, a dual-resolution codec-based architecture for lexicon-free Malay speech synthesis. The model expands character representations at a temporal resolution of 50 Hz and subsequently downsamples them through strided convolution to 12.5 Hz for discrete codec-token prediction. Objective evaluations show that the proposed model reduces the character error rate (CER) from 27.11% for the baseline to 21.86%, an absolute reduction of 5.25 percentage points. The proposed model also achieves a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.30, compared with 4.12 for the baseline. These results suggest that the dual-resolution design may improve character-level alignment and perceived speech naturalness under the evaluated conditions.

title: Geometric Time Score Estimators: Bridging Self-Predictive Representations and Generative Occupancy Models For Reinforcement Learning
text: In reinforcement learning (RL), temporal reasoning is essential for estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure. While self-predictive representations have been a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation, we find that they yield surprisingly poor estimates. On the other hand, generative occupancy models can produce remarkably accurate samples from the occupancy measure. Yet, they cannot easily recover occupancy densities, limiting their use for control despite their expressivity. In this paper, we propose Geometric Time Score Estimators (GTSE), a framework that bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths. We analyze how GTSE implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning and show how to directly extract self-predictive representations from this framework. Through experiments across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, we show that GTSE improves performance over state-of-the-art methods by formula to formula in goal-conditioned RL settings, and that the representations learned using our framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks. Website: https://aravindvenu7.github.io/website/gtse/

title:
The Equilibrium Structure of Cosmological Halos: From Dwarf Galaxies to
  X-ray Clusters
text: A new model for the postcollapse equilibrium structure of virialized objects which condense out of the cosmological background universe is described and compared with observations and simulations of cosmological halos from dwarf galaxies to X-ray clusters. The model is based upon the assumption that virialized halos are isothermal, which leads to a prediction of a unique nonsingular isothermal sphere for the equilibrium structure, with a core radius which is approximately 1/30 times the size and a core density which is proportional to the mean background density at the epoch of collapse. These predicted nonsingular isothermal spheres are in good agreement with the observations of the internal structure of dark-matter-dominated halos from dwarf galaxies to X-ray clusters.

title:
Adiabatic Losses and Stochastic Particle Acceleration in Gamma-Ray Burst
  Blast Waves
text: We treat the problem of adiabatic losses and stochastic particle acceleration in gamma-ray burst (GRB) blast waves that decelerate by sweeping up matter from an external medium. The shocked fluid is assumed to be represented by a homogeneous expanding shell. The energy lost by nonthermal particles through adiabatic expansion is converted to the bulk kinetic energy of the outflow, permitting the evolution of the bulk Lorentz factor Gamma of the blast wave to be self-consistently calculated. The behavior of the system is shown to reproduce the hydrodynamic self-similar solutions in the relativistic and nonrelativistic limits, and the formalism is applicable to scenarios that are intermediate between the adiabatic and fully radiative regimes. Nonthermal particle energization through stochastic gyroresonant acceleration with magnetic turbulence in the blast wave is treated by employing energy-gain rates and diffusive escape timescales based upon expressions derived in the quasilinear regime. If the magnetic field in the shocked fluid approaches its equipartition value, this process can accelerate escaping particles to >~10^20 eV energies, consistent with the hypothesis that ultra-high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are accelerated by GRB blast waves. Due to particle trapping by the magnetic turbulence, only the highest energy particles can escape during the prompt and afterglow phases of a GRB for acceleration by a Kolmogorov spectrum of MHD turbulence. Lower energy particles begin to escape as the blast wave becomes nonrelativistic and shock Fermi acceleration becomes more important.

title: Predicted Planck Extragalactic Point Source Catalogue
text: An estimation of the number and amplitude (in flux) of the extragalactic point sources that will be observed by the Planck Mission is presented in this paper. The study is based on the Mexican Hat wavelet formalism introduced by Cayon et al. 2000.
